sources.news_title: White House asks Guilfoyle to step down as ambassador to Greece after 8 months of alleged pay-for-access schemes: 'absolutely was a quid pro quo'
sources.text:
Kimberly Guilfoyle is stepping down as the US ambassador to Greece following a series of reports alleging she sought payment from a donor in exchange for access to administration officials. The White House announced the decision on Tuesday morning, effectively ending the diplomatic tenure of one of President Donald Trump’s most prominent political allies after only eight months in the role.
The White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, confirmed the news during her first briefing on Tuesday. She said, “We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign, she has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well.”
While Guilfoyle confirmed her departure after media uproar, she described the position as the “honor of a lifetime” and denied the allegations against her as “false.” In a post on social media, she stated, “While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end.” She also pledged to “vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
The controversy centers on claims that Guilfoyle leveraged her position for personal gain
Reports indicate that in July 2025, days before her Senate confirmation hearing, she pressured donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 American Express bill. According to the reports, she assured him the transfer would not be traceable, writing, “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.”
Guilfoyle allegedly offered to use her influence regarding his tax and legal issues, claiming she had contacted the IRS commissioner and the Justice Department on his behalf. Deters has stated he paid Guilfoyle about $300,000 over the years without receiving any favors, telling MS Now that the request “absolutely was a quid pro quo.”
Guilfoyle’s lawyer, Jesse Binnall, has stated that she disputes the authenticity of the messages. Even so, the allegations have been extensive. Reports have suggested she accepted improper gifts, promoted the interests of a Greek company named Aktor during official engagements, and allegedly threatened a host-country official.
One particularly damaging claim suggested she told the Greek energy minister that Washington could topple the local government if they did not align with her interests. This caused significant outrage in Greece, leading the country’s foreign minister, Giorgos Gerapetritis, to address the matter during a parliamentary debate on October 9.
The situation created significant friction within the administration. Sources indicate that both President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio became furious over the allegations. Former senior US diplomat Alec Mally noted that the embassy in Athens was placed in an impossible situation, describing Guilfoyle’s behavior as reminiscent of an old-style Balkan country. He added, “It would not surprise me if the Greek public reacts with joy to the news of her resignation.”
Guilfoyle, 57, a former San Francisco prosecutor, became a staple of the Trump political orbit after joining the campaign in 2018. Following a lengthy nomination process that required Republicans to use the “nuclear option” in September 2025 to overcome a filibuster, she arrived in Athens in late October 2025. Her time there was marked by unconventional behavior, including visits to local music clubs shortly after her arrival.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump considers firing Donald Trump Jr.'s ex-fiancée amid $100K allegations
sources.text:
President Donald Trump is considering firing Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., from her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece.
The possible move comes as Guilfoyle faces questions over allegations that she sought $100,000 from a Republican donor while discussing access to senior figures in the Trump administration.
Trump publicly confirmed that Guilfoyle’s future was under review when reporters asked him about the controversy at the White House. “We’re looking at it,” Trump said, before adding that his administration was “not happy.”
For now, Guilfoyle remains ambassador, and the White House has not announced a final decision on her position.
The $100,000 allegation at the center of the dispute
Much of the controversy involves businessman and Trump supporter Eric Deters.
He claims Guilfoyle asked him to help cover a $100,000 American Express bill before her Senate confirmation hearing in 2025. Deters has also alleged that their discussions involved possible introductions to powerful people connected to the administration.
Deters says he never paid the money. Messages reportedly provided by him have become a key part of the story, but Guilfoyle’s attorneys dispute his account and have challenged the authenticity and meaning of the communications.
No public finding has established that Guilfoyle committed a crime, making it important to separate the allegations from proven facts.
Guilfoyle’s lawyers strongly reject the accusations
Her legal team says the financial dispute has been presented without proper context.
Attorneys representing Guilfoyle argue that any money discussed with Deters involved compensation she believed she was owed for professional appearances and speaking engagements arranged before she became ambassador. They deny that she tried to exchange government access for personal payment.
That distinction could become central to any official review. Being paid for legitimate work completed before entering government service would be very different from offering political access in return for money.
Determining what was promised, when the work occurred, and what the requested payment actually covered could shape how seriously the administration treats the matter.
Questions extend beyond the disputed payment
Guilfoyle has also faced scrutiny over reports concerning private flights, luxury travel, and her relationships with wealthy business figures in Greece.
Questions have been raised about whether any of those connections overlapped with her diplomatic responsibilities or created potential conflicts while she represented the United States abroad.
Her attorneys have pushed back against those claims as well. They say Guilfoyle sought State Department guidance concerning private travel and followed applicable ethics requirements.
The details matter because accepting transportation or hospitality does not automatically establish wrongdoing. Approval, disclosure, purpose, and the circumstances surrounding each trip would all need examination.
Her history with the Trump family adds another layer
Guilfoyle’s place inside Trump’s political circle began years before her diplomatic appointment.
A former California prosecutor and Fox News personality, she started dating Donald Trump Jr. in 2018. Their relationship quickly became public, with Guilfoyle appearing regularly at campaign events and becoming a prominent fundraiser and speaker for Trump’s political movement.
The couple eventually became engaged but separated in 2024. Guilfoyle nevertheless remained connected to Trump’s political operation.
Trump nominated her as ambassador to Greece in December 2024, shortly after reports emerged that her relationship with Donald Trump Jr. had ended. She was later confirmed by the Senate in 2025.
The Greece appointment raised Guilfoyle’s responsibilities
Becoming ambassador moved Guilfoyle from partisan campaigning into a formal diplomatic job.
An ambassador speaks for the United States, deals with foreign officials, and helps manage sensitive political, economic, and security relationships. That makes questions involving money, business contacts, or access especially serious, even when the underlying accusations remain disputed.
Greece is an important American partner in southeastern Europe, with cooperation covering defense, regional security, shipping, and energy.
Any prolonged controversy surrounding Washington’s top representative in Athens risks becoming more than a personal political problem. It can distract from the diplomatic work the ambassador was appointed to handle.
Marco Rubio has also been pulled into the story
Secretary of State Marco Rubio recently visited Athens while questions about Guilfoyle were gaining attention. She appeared alongside him during official events.
When reporters raised the allegations, Rubio initially questioned whether the reporting had been sufficiently established and avoided publicly condemning the ambassador based on claims that remained contested.
Later reports suggested frustration inside the administration had grown. Trump’s own acknowledgment that he was reviewing Guilfoyle’s future moved the story beyond outside speculation.
Instead of simply defending a political ally, the president openly left the possibility of dismissal on the table, putting new pressure on Guilfoyle to answer the accusations.

sources.news_title: Trump Asks Guilfoyle to Resign as Greece Ambassador
sources.text:
President Trump said he asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as U.S. ambassador to Greece because the White House “didn’t like what we were reading” about misconduct claims.
New White House press secretary Katie Zacharia used her first briefing Tuesday to confirm the request. Guilfoyle is stepping down from the Greece post after a flurry of reports about money, access, and embassy conduct.
Trump drew a clear line when reporters pressed him. He praised the work she had done in Athens, then made plain he would not carry the baggage of the stories now surrounding her.
“No, she wasn't a member of my family. She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago,” Trump told reporters. “She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading.”
Fox News reported that Zacharia framed the exit in warm but final terms, calling Guilfoyle “a wonderful asset to the team” while confirming the president had asked her to resign.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."
That language matched the White House pattern of separating past loyalty from present standards. The decision followed less than a week of damaging coverage tied to a donor and a large credit-card bill.
The core trigger was a report detailing text messages reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. In a July 3, 2025 exchange, Guilfoyle allegedly pressed Trump donor Eric Deters for $100,000 to pay off her American Express card.
One message attributed to her read: “Honey, please I need you to get this done for me today.” Deters, who was seeking administration attention for personal tax and legal issues, reportedly did not hand over the money.
The timing mattered. Those texts came days before Guilfoyle’s July 9, 2025 Senate confirmation hearing for the Greece ambassadorship. Asking a donor for personal cash while chasing a diplomatic post is the kind of optics no serious administration can shrug off.
The New York Post added that the Journal account also described talk of wiring funds in a way that would not show up, and noted separate scrutiny over Guilfoyle’s ties to lobbyist Christos Marafatsos, Greek firm Aktor Group, and shipping tycoon Nikolas Tsakos.
Additional allegations circulating with the exit included promoting foreign business interests and harsh treatment of embassy staff. None of that had to be proven in court for the White House to decide the relationship was no longer tenable.
Guilfoyle rejected the claims in full. On X she said the accusations were false and that she would defend her name and record.
"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional."
She added that she would not let “false accusations” define decades of public service. In other remarks she called the ambassadorship “the honor of a lifetime” and thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio “for entrusting me with the extraordinary privilege of representing the greatest country in the history of the world.”
The Washington Examiner reported her further pledge that even as the diplomatic role ends, her commitment to Trump, the America First movement, and the country “will never end.”
"While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end."
That is the posture of someone trying to leave the stage without burning the bridge. It does not erase the texts, the donor ask, or the staff and business-interest questions now attached to her short tenure.
Guilfoyle’s path into Trump world ran through Donald Trump Jr. The two were engaged for nearly four years before a late 2024 split, shortly after Trump won a second term. A source told People it was “a friendly split” and that the family remained “enamored with” her at the time. Dating rumors linking Trump Jr. and Bettina Anderson, now his wife, had already begun swirling in December 2024.
Trump’s answer to reporters shut that door for good. She was not family. She had dated his son “a long time ago.” She had done a good job in Greece. And still, the reading material was bad enough to end the appointment.
That sequence is accountability, not drama. Ambassadors represent the United States. When private money, access, and embassy conduct become the story, the president’s job is to protect the office, not the résumé of a former campaign surrogate and ex-Fox News host who once worked as a California prosecutor.
Zacharia’s first briefing made the personnel move official. Guilfoyle’s own statements made her exit public. Trump’s comments made the reason unmistakable: the reports were not something the White House would own or explain away.
Personnel is policy. When the reading turns sour, the smart move is to close the book and move on.

sources.news_title: Guilfoyle resigns as ambassador to Greece – adding to the global vacancies sapping US embassies
sources.text:
The United States is down one more ambassador. On Oct. 13, 2026, it emerged that President Donald Trump had asked Kimberly Guilfoyle, a MAGA loyalist and ex-fiancée of Trump’s son Donald Jr., to resign her position as U.S. ambassador to Greece, a NATO ally. It follows allegations that the Trump adviser turned diplomat pushed for a Republican donor to pay off her six-figure American Express bill.
Guilfoyle later confirmed that she would comply with the request and resigned. In so doing, Athens became one of a number of U.S. overseas missions with a vacancy at the top. In fact, 93 out of 196 U.S. ambassador jobs are currently unfilled.
And that is after U.S. senators confirmed 10 new ambassadors before leaving town on Sept. 30, 2026. Among those nodded through before Congress closed for an extended midterm recess were new U.S. ambassadors for Kenya, Nicaragua, Malaysia and Kyrgyzstan.
With some of the vacancies the White House has not even sent names to Capitol Hill, despite the second Trump administration being a year and a half into the job. Withn others, the Senate, which is controlled by the same party as the White House, hasn’t acted on the names put forward. Should the Athens position be added to the list, the reason will be down to potential insufficient vetting or an ill-advised appointing strategy that promotes loyalty over experience.
Regardless of the reason, as a former ambassador and an expert in the process of diplomacy, I find the current vacancies concerning. Among those embassies still without a top person in place are key partners for the U.S. – countries that Washington needs to achieve its security, economic and strategic objectives.
What makes these vacancies more worrying, in my view, is that they come amid other concerning developments in the State Department’s staffing of embassies.
Politicizing diplomacy
Chief among them are the high percentage of politically appointed ambassadors relative to positions filled by career diplomats – that is, senior foreign service officers, usually with at least 20 years of diplomatic experience.
Though many countries send politicians abroad as ambassadors, America’s diplomatic service is unique in two ways. The percentage of U.S. ambassadors who are political appointees – those who haven’t followed a career civil service path – is higher than comparative countries across the world. Second, those political appointees are often donors with little to no government experience.
The practice has existed for decades, but in recent years the number of political appointees has increased. During the Obama administration, the percentage of political appointees was around 30%. The number rose to around 40% in the first Trump administration and the subsequent Biden administration.
But in Trump’s second term, some 80% of names the White House has sent to the Senate have been political.
And many of the people Trump has put forward don’t appear to have the credentials usually associated with holding important diplomatic positions. Rather, many are friends, associates or donors to Trump, often with little overseas experience or knowledge of the country they are going to.
Lee Lipton, ambassador to a key ally in the Philippines, is owner of a restaurant in Palm Beach – Florida Benny’s on the Beach – a member of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago Club and a contributor to his political campaign.
The system of political appointees has always had an element of handing ambassadorships to friends and supporters. But what has changed under Trump is the range of positions now available. In the past, ambassadors to key countries like Chile, Israel, Peru, the Philippines, Turkey and Egypt, for example, have almost always been career appointees. This has changed under the second Trump administration.
Appointing noncareer diplomats to small, faraway nations has the additional problem that the chosen individual may not actually spend much time there. The rule of thumb has long been that ambassadors should spend no more than one month every year back in the United States. But that is compromised if a noncareer diplomat with expansive business ties in the U.S. is selected.
The role of a deputy
A closely related problem is the State Department’s handling of an ambassador’s second in command, their deputy chiefs of missions – DCMs for short – under Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
During Trump’s first term in the White House, politically appointed ambassadors were often encouraged to swap out the DCMs they inherited from their predecessors. It meant going through a long hiring process, leaving those key jobs unfilled for months.
In 2025, the State Department went further, canceling the assignments of senior officers en route to take up embassy jobs and opening a new hiring process.
It formed part of a Trump purge of what many MAGA Republicans characterized as a “deep state” civil service. The reality is that DCMs fill a critically important role in helping political appointees navigate the bureaucracy and implement their policy ideas, as well as raising the occasional reality check.
With more politically appointed ambassadors – some of them with no relevant experience – having an experienced DCM can be the difference between success and failure.
Looking for other friends
When you put all of these personnel changes together, the result is the degradation of what was once seen as one of the most effective diplomatic services in the world.
What makes this potentially more worrying is where the vacancies are. For example, Belarus and Bulgaria, neighbors to Russia and Ukraine, are without U.S. ambassadors. And important countries in the fight against terrorism or in geopolitical hot spots, such as Kuwait, Qatar and Mauritania, are in the same camp.
Other countries still without ambassadors include Indonesia, Southeast Asia’s largest nation and the most populous Muslim-majority country in the world; key Middle East ally Egypt and nuclear power Pakistan; and nations the U.S. needs to help manage inward migration, such us Haiti and Guatemala.
The problem of absent or inexperienced ambassadors goes both ways. It means Washington may not have a capable diplomatic figurehead in these countries to contact in times of need. There are also fewer avenues for host nations to successfully convey messages back to the U.S. administration.
When faced with absent ambassadors, amateurish political appointees and deputy mission chiefs who are very junior or career appointees with short resumes, host countries may conclude that they aren’t seen as important to the U.S. and start looking elsewhere for friends.
And the U.S. has hollowed out its ambassadorial corps at a time when it is facing growing international influence by the likes of Russia, China and Iran – rival nations hoping to capitalize on a perceived diplomatic void left by Washington.
For example, as the U.S. tries to contain Beijing’s influence in the Asia-Pacific region, Fiji, Indonesia and Laos remain without U.S. ambassadors. Similarly, China’s diplomatic relations with Pakistan – a former key security partner for Washington – have grown while the ambassadorial seat in Islamabad remains empty.
And former Soviet states including Georgia and Kazakhstan don’t have U.S. ambassadors even as Russia President Vladimir Putin attempts to consolidate Moscow’s regional influence.
In large areas of the world, such as Africa and the Pacific region, and in important areas of policy, the lights may be on in U.S. embassies, but nobody’s home. And that is a distinct problem for national security and strategic interests.

sources.text:
Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, according to White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, was facing mounting scrutiny over reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to the administration and behaved inappropriately while in Athens.
Trump said on Tuesday that she had done a good job, but will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.
Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself, calling the claims false, and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".
Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.
Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
Around the same time, news broke that she had broken up with Donald Trump Jr, to whom she was engaged.
In a lengthy post on X on Tuesday, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.
"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".
Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on behalf of Deters before she became ambassador.
Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.
Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".
Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.
Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with Trump Jr. They became engaged in 2018 and broke up in late 2024.
Trump said on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member.
The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign.
"She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.
Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.
For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration saw as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family, and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.
She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

Trump Fired Kimberly Guilfoyle for Influence Peddling That Pales Next to His Presidential Profiteering
If the former ambassador tried to use her office for personal gain, she was only imitating her boss.
Kimberly Guilfoyle today resigned from her position as the U.S. ambassador to Greece shortly after the White House confirmed that President Donald Trump had asked her to do so. The main provocation seems to have been Guilfoyle's alleged influence peddling, which reportedly featured a request that Republican donor Eric Deters pay off her $100,000 American Express bill, in exchange for which she promised him special access to "Trump world."
The president signaled his displeasure on Monday, saying "we're looking at" axing Guilfoyle, his son's former girlfriend, because "we're not happy." On Tuesday, Trump added that "we didn't like what we were reading." That reaction is not surprising, since Guilfoyle would have been horning in on Trump's territory by trying to sell access and use her office for personal gain. That's his thing.
Consider Trump's attempts to promote the memecoin that he launched three days before beginning his second term. That April, the top 220 $TRUMP holders were invited to "an intimate private dinner" with the president on May 22. The "top 25 coin holders" were promised "an Exclusive Reception before Dinner with YOUR FAVORITE PRESIDENT," plus a "Special VIP Tour" of the White House the next day. The coin's price, which after an initial surge had fallen dramatically since Inauguration Day, rose by more than 50 percent immediately after that announcement.
"Since the announcement, crypto investors around the world have raced to expand their holdings of $TRUMP," The New York Times reported 10 days before the dinner. "Certain buyers, in interviews and statements, have said they bought the coins or entered the dinner contest with the intention of securing an action by Mr. Trump to affect United States policy."
NBC reported that the coin investors who attended the dinner, which was held at the Trump National Golf Club in Sterling, Virginia, had collectively spent $394 million on $TRUMP. On average, that worked out to about $1.8 million a plate.
"This is my president that we're talking about, but I am willing to say that this gives me pause," Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R–Wyo.) said a few weeks before the dinner. "In abstract," Sen. Thom Tillis (R–N.C.) allowed, the event "is hard to understand." Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R–Alaska) drew an analogy: "I don't think it would be appropriate for me to charge people to come into the Capitol and take a tour."
Donald Sherman, executive director of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, was blunter. "This is one of the most blatant and appalling instances of selling access to the presidency I've ever seen," he said.
Compared to that episode, the controversy over the income that Trump's hotel in Washington, D.C., received from influence seekers during his first term might seem tame. But it raised similar ethical questions, albeit in a slightly more subtle way.
The Trump International Hotel's customers included Republican political organizations and a long list of trade groups, such as the National Mining Association, the Independent Petroleum Association of America, the National Confectioners Association, and the Vapor Technology Association, whose interests might be served by currying favor with the president. The hotel also attracted business from the governments of foreign countries, such as Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Azerbaijan, Malaysia, and Romania, that likewise may have been investing in Trump's good will.
"Believe me, all the delegations will go there," a "Middle Eastern diplomat" told The Washington Post after Trump's election. "Why wouldn't I stay at his hotel blocks from the White House, so I can tell the new president, 'I love your new hotel!'" an "Asian diplomat" said. "Isn't it rude to come to his city and say, 'I am staying at your competitor'?" The Embassy of Kuwait, which had previously held its annual National Day celebration at the Four Seasons, reportedly canceled its reservation there and switched to the president-elect's hotel under pressure from the Trump Organization.
Trump saw no problem with any of this. "The law is totally on my side," he told The New York Times in November 2016. "The president can't have a conflict of interest." He reiterated that take at a press conference nine days before his inauguration. "I have a no-conflict situation because I'm president," he said.
Trump nevertheless said he would donate the profits from money spent by foreign governments at his hotels to the U.S. Treasury. But that solution did not address the money he was taking in from various domestic interest groups or his ability to enrich himself by encouraging Republican organizations or other federal officials to patronize his businesses.
One example of the latter: Vice President Mike Pence and his party stayed at Trump's golf resort in Doonbeg, Ireland, during an official trip in 2019. Although Trump insisted he "had nothing to do" with that decision, critics perceived a violation of the Domestic Emoluments Clause, which says the president may not receive additional compensation from the federal government beyond his official salary.
Trump later said he regretted his attempts to address conflicts of interest during his first term, including his promise that the Trump Organization would avoid new foreign business deals. "I prohibited [my sons] from doing business in my first term, and I got absolutely no credit for it," he told The New York Times 12 days before his second inauguration. "I didn't have to do that, and it's really unfair to them." The lesson he drew was that "nobody cared."
Consistent with that assessment, Trump has thrown all caution to the wind during his second term, capitalizing on his position to rake in millions of dollars by hawking all manner of presidentially branded merchandise, ranging from bibles to cologne; obtain a $400 million "palace in the sky" from the government of Qatar; extort $1 billion in pro bono legal work from disfavored law firms; earn billions from the same cryptocurrency industry he was simultaneously deregulating; and arrange a sweet IRS immunity deal that could save him more than $100 million in back taxes, interest, and penalties. Any worries about unseemly profiteering by Trump's family are long gone, as evidenced by federal contracts with businesses backed by his sons and highly lucrative foreign deals negotiated by his son-in-law.
Compared to all of that, the $100,000 that Guilfoyle allegedly sought in exchange for using her influence with the Trump administration to help Deters looks like pocket change. Her real sin, one suspects, was failing to offer her boss a piece of the action.

Kimberly Guilfoyle Resigns as Trump’s Ambassador to Greece After White House Demands Her Departure Amid $100,000 Scandal
Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as U.S. ambassador to Greece on Tuesday after President Trump requested her departure following allegations that she solicited $100,000 from a Republican donor to pay a personal credit card bill in exchange for access to senior administration officials.
The resignation marks a sudden end to the diplomatic appointment of one of Trump’s longtime political allies. Guilfoyle, a former Fox News personality and former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., had come under increasing scrutiny over allegations involving her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy Greek businessmen.
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia confirmed Tuesday morning that the administration had formally requested Guilfoyle’s resignation. The announcement came during Zacharia’s first official briefing since replacing Karoline Leavitt.
Zacharia acknowledged Guilfoyle’s contributions to the administration and wished her well but made clear that the decision to seek her departure had already been made.
The announcement followed several days of discussions within the administration about whether Guilfoyle should remain in her diplomatic position. President Trump had publicly acknowledged Monday that he was considering removing her following reports about her alleged conduct.
Speaking with reporters outside the White House, Trump expressed dissatisfaction with the allegations and indicated that the administration was reviewing the situation.
By Tuesday, the president had reached a decision. Trump told reporters that Guilfoyle had performed well in certain aspects of her job but acknowledged that the administration was troubled by the emerging reports.
The president also distanced himself from Guilfoyle’s previous personal relationship with his family, pointing out that she had dated his son but was not a member of the Trump family.
Guilfoyle responded to the resignation request with a lengthy public statement defending her reputation, expressing gratitude to Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and reaffirming her commitment to the president’s political movement.
She described serving as ambassador to Greece as an extraordinary honor and thanked the administration for allowing her to represent the United States abroad.
Despite the circumstances surrounding her departure, Guilfoyle emphasized that her political loyalty remained unchanged.
She pledged to continue supporting President Trump and his America First agenda even after leaving her diplomatic position, making clear that the controversy would not end her involvement in conservative politics.
Guilfoyle also strongly rejected allegations that she had used her diplomatic appointment for personal financial benefit. She described the accusations as false and vowed to defend her name and professional reputation.
Her resignation followed a series of reports detailing allegations of questionable financial arrangements before and during her tenure as ambassador.
The most serious accusations involve former Republican congressional candidate and Trump supporter Eric Deters, who claims Guilfoyle requested $100,000 to pay an outstanding American Express credit card bill in July 2025.
According to messages provided by Deters, Guilfoyle allegedly urged him to transfer the money directly to American Express shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.
Deters claims the request was connected to promises that Guilfoyle would help him gain access to influential officials within the Trump administration.
He has characterized the arrangement as an attempted exchange of money for political influence, although he maintains that he ultimately refused to make the requested payment.
Deters also claims he had previously paid Guilfoyle substantial sums for appearances and other services while seeking assistance with business and legal matters.
Guilfoyle’s attorneys have disputed his characterization of their financial relationship. They maintain that the money she sought represented legitimate compensation for public appearances and speaking engagements that had not been paid.
Her legal representatives have also challenged the authenticity of certain communications attributed to her and rejected allegations that she attempted to improperly exchange political access for personal financial benefit.
The controversy expanded beyond the disputed credit card payment as additional allegations emerged about Guilfoyle’s conduct in Greece.
Reports raised questions about her relationship with Christos Marafatsos, a lobbyist associated with the Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group.
Guilfoyle allegedly promoted the company’s business interests during diplomatic engagements and allowed Marafatsos to participate in meetings involving American officials.
Those reports prompted concerns about whether a private company’s representatives had received unusual access to diplomatic discussions through their relationship with the ambassador.
Additional scrutiny focused on Guilfoyle’s connections to wealthy Greek businessmen, including shipping executive Nikolas Tsakos.
Reports described luxury travel arrangements, private aircraft and hospitality allegedly provided by individuals with business interests that could intersect with American diplomatic activities.
Guilfoyle’s attorneys have maintained that she followed State Department guidance concerning travel and accepted transportation only after seeking appropriate approval.
Other allegations involved remarks she reportedly made about the United States’ ability to influence political developments in Greece. Those claims have also been disputed.
The growing controversy reportedly frustrated Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece last week for diplomatic engagements and appeared alongside Guilfoyle.
Rubio initially defended her performance, describing her as a strong ambassador. However, he later declined to address specific allegations without confirming their accuracy.
The State Department’s Office of Inspector General has also been examining concerns surrounding Guilfoyle’s conduct, although officials have not publicly announced findings establishing wrongdoing.
Congressional Democrats have demanded additional scrutiny of the allegations, including questions about potential conflicts of interest and the use of diplomatic authority to benefit private individuals or businesses.
Among those seeking further examination are Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, Rep. Gregory Meeks and Rep. Robert Garcia, who have called for greater accountability regarding the ambassador’s reported activities.
Guilfoyle’s departure is particularly notable because of her longstanding relationship with President Trump and his political organization.
Before becoming ambassador, she worked as a California prosecutor, built a national profile as a television personality and became a prominent Republican fundraiser and campaign surrogate.
She was previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom before entering a relationship with Donald Trump Jr. The couple became engaged in 2020 but separated in 2024.
Trump nominated Guilfoyle to serve as ambassador to Greece following their separation, placing her in a diplomatically significant position involving NATO cooperation, regional security and energy development.
Her appointment was viewed as an opportunity for a longtime political supporter to represent the administration in a strategically important European country.
However, the allegations that emerged during her tenure eventually created sufficient concern within the White House for the president to request her resignation.
Guilfoyle has not been charged with a crime, and the accusations involving her financial dealings and diplomatic conduct remain disputed. Her departure does not constitute a legal finding that she violated federal law.
The administration has not announced who will replace her as ambassador or when a successor might be nominated.
For President Trump, the decision removes a politically connected appointee whose conduct had become the subject of increasing scrutiny. It also demonstrates that even longtime allies can lose administration positions when allegations generate substantial controversy.
Guilfoyle, meanwhile, has made clear that she intends to challenge the accusations and remain involved in the political movement she has supported for years.
Although her time representing the United States in Greece has come to an end, her statement indicates that she considers the dispute over her reputation far from settled.

While U.S. ambassadors can be recalled by the president at any time, it is more unusual for an individual ambassador to be specifically asked to resign. Career diplomats who are recalled from ambassadorial posts can remain in the Foreign Service and return to Washington for other assignments.
In 2012, Obama appointee and former Air Force major general Scott Gration resigned as U.S. ambassador to Kenya, attributing the decision to "differences with Washington regarding my leadership style and certain priorities."
In 2020, Trump removed Gordon Sondland as U.S. ambassador to the European Union. He had been a major witness in the president's first impeachment inquiry. Months earlier, Sondland's attorney had said he had "no intention of resigning."
In February 2020, two days after the Senate acquitted Trump, Sondland said: "I was advised today that the President intends to recall me effective immediately as United States Ambassador to the European Union."

sources.news_title: Trump asks Greece Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign after allegations of improper conduct: White House
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigned on Tuesday after allegations of improper conduct but insisted she’ll “vigorously defend” herself.
Trump’s administration said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.
The announcement, after days of comments and speculation, came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle “has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”
Guilfoyle’s departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct.
“Well, we’re looking at it,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he was considering firing Guilfoyle. “We’re not happy.”
Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on her future this week.
In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.
Guilfoyle denies the accusations and cites her ‘decades of public service’
Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in a post on X, saying, “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”
“I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”
In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle’s lawyers denied she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.
The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle’s travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she “sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department’s travel regulations.”
The allegations began surfacing weeks ago
After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.”
But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.
“You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.
A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.
The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal.
The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.
There was no immediate response to Zacharia’s statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.
Ahead of Tuesday’s announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. “This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity,” Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated “the same way as every other ambassador” and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.
Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa’s “Dance the Night,” from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie “Barbie.”
Democrats call for an investigation
The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.
Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.
The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.
Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.
Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco’s mayor, before he became California’s governor. She later was engaged to Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr.
___
AP journalist Derek Gatopoulos in Athens contributed.
